newsitem.title: POLAND: Poles clean up damage as flood recedes.
newsitem.headline: Poles clean up damage as flood recedes.

text.p: After a month of fighting the worst floods in centuries, Polish rescue teams were shifting efforts on Wednesday from reinforcing sodden dikes on the swollen Oder River to clean-up work and food distribution.

The government press office said the danger of flooding still existed in the western towns of Nowa Sol and Slubice across from Germany's Frankfurt an der Oder where water still exceeded flood alert levels by between 1.5 to 2 metres.
"The water is easing slowly, more than a dozen centimetres a day, but the danger of flooding exists as long as the river does not return to its riverbed," it said in a statement.
"The dikes are so sodden that there is a constant danger they will break despite continuous reinforcement work, but the worst is over," it added.
The office said rescue teams were currently working in eight Polish provinces, compared with 14 when the disaster, which killed 54 people, was at its worst in July.

"At the peak of the action there were almost 80,000 people taking part in the rescue efforts. Currently there are still some 37,000 workers engaged in pumping out water and cleaning buildings and delivering food and medicine," the office said.
It said 1,700 sq km were still swamped against a total of 6,660 sq km inundated since early July, and more than 37,000 people were still displaced.
The government has so far projected flood relief expenses at close to $2 billion, but more precise estimates are not likely to be available until the second half of August.

The clean-up efforts began taking centre stage in large cities, such as the south-western Wroclaw, where the receding waters left behind a plague of mosquitoes breeding on the innumerable pools of still water left by the retreating river.
The city was also infested by rats, feeding on garbage strewn on the streets by the flood.

"The town will start getting rid of the rats as soon as all the water subsides and the garbage is removed so that the animals don't have anything else to eat but rat-poison," said Janusz Tarkowski epidemiologist at the Health Ministry.
He said that despite the difficult sanitary situation in the affected towns, no major epidemics wre expected.
